speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister indicated earlier that he considered there to be only one official in Parliament who could deal with the question of the Minister's conduct in relation to the Elections Act and he referred to the Elections Act official.
How does that square with the statement which he made and the position he took in the conflict of interest guidelines wherein he said that the responsibility for the ethical conduct of his Ministers would not be sloughed off to other officials, other members of the Government, but that he would be responsible as Prime Minister for the ethical conduct of his Ministers? Has he discharged that responsibility in relation to this particular Minister?
Allegations have been made and not answered. Conflicting evidence has been presented about what the Minister said and what he did with his lawyer. Where is the Prime Minister with his responsibility for the ethical behaviour of his Ministers?

subtopic: ETHICAL CONDUCT OF MINISTERS-PRIME MINISTER'S RESPONSIBILITY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there is a statute that governs the conduct of Members of Parliament in respect of election activity. That statute, passed by Members of this House, provides for an officer, in the event of a charge being laid or an accusation being made, to investigate charges relating to a Member of Parliament. It also provides thereafter, pursuant to the evidence, for charges being laid against a Member of Parliament unless the commissioner comes to the conclusion that the allegations do not sustain the laying of a charge.
Charges were made after the last election and investigations were conducted of members of all political Parties in this House. Pursuant to the law the commissioner conducted investigations and arrived at conclusions with regard to whether to lay charges, yes or no.
In the case of the Member for Frontenac or the case of the Member for Hamilton East or others-

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Prime Minister and relates again to his responsibility as the Prime Minister. He knows that there is a discrepancy between what Mr. Masse has said to be the truth and what Mr. Guilbeault has said to be the truth.

January 28, 1988

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member's Leader has already referred to the letter in question as an unusual one. That is an understatement, for the very simple reason that under our system of British common law charges are either laid or they are not.
Charges are recommended under this statute by an independent officer of Parliament. The independent officer of Parliament came to the conclusion that Mr. Masse should not be charged. In the course of conveying that formal opinion he also put out a point of view on a provision of the statute.
I cannot explain why that was done in a manner in which I believe would make it difficult for any Member of Parliament to defend himself or herself, because no charges were laid. The only person who can tell you why he did that, may I say respectfully, is Mr. Gorman, which is why we have suggested that this go to a parliamentary committee so that my hon. friend can ask Mr. Gorman. Once Mr. Gorman has responded, perhaps we can consider the matter again.

Mr. Speaker, just to show the carelessness of the accusations and the reason why I hope we will be very prudent in the assessments of statements, my hon. friend just said that Mr. Guilbeault said that Mr. Masse is not telling the truth. The important consideration, if you believe in justice, is that the reputation of someone who has not been accused of a crime or accused of an offence is being tarnished on the floor of the House of Commons. He is being subject to attack, innuendo and character assassination, but cannot defend himself in the
absence of a formal charge which is fundamental to the nature of our system of justice. All I am saying is to either charge the Member of Parliament or not. If you have any problems with it, cause the man who has the concerns to come before the House of Commons or a committee thereof and explain why. Surely that is fundamental and elementary to our system of justice.

speechtext:

January 28, 1988

subsubtopic: SUPREME COURT DECISION-REQUEST FOR MEETING OF FEDERAL AND PROVINCIAL MINISTERS

The House resumed, from Wednesday, January 27, consideration of the motion of Mr. Bouchard:

Amendment 4 would exclude only criminals and war criminals from the refugee determination process, but would allow terrorists, spies and subversives to pursue a claim to refugee status, notwithstanding the fact that Article 33 of the UN Convention would permit the removal of these latter individuals to their countries of nationality or permanent residence, even if they were determined to be Convention refugees.
Amendment 5(a) would eliminate the authority of the Minister to direct a ship to leave or not to enter Canadian waters. This amendment would reopen a significant gap in Canada's ability to control its borders.
Amendments 5(b) and (c) arise out of Senate amendment 5(a), which is not acceptable, and are therefore inappropriate.
Amendments 6(a) and (b) would reverse the policy on which the Immigration Act, 1976 was based, which policy was not changed in the Bill as passed by this House. Mr. Speaker, I notice Members on the Government side are in a hurry, but that should not keep us from expressing our views in the House on legislation as important as Bill C-84.
Mr. Speaker, first of all, I would like to provide some background on Bill C-84 and remind Hon. Members and Canadians that we came back during the summer because there was an emergency-remember? There was a national emergency because one morning, a hundred or so refugees were found on the shores of Nova Scotia. Once the House had been reconvened to introduce this Bill, the Government took its own sweet time, giving various excuses for the subsequent delay. The result is that today, in January 1988-I am sure you will agree, Mr. Speaker, that between August 1987 and January 1988, there was no national emergency, and if the Government intended to amend the Immigration Act, if it intended to table a new immigration policy for this country, it could have done so during our regular session without rushing things, without the phony excuse that we were faced with a national emergency in this country.
Mr. Speaker, Canada and Canadians are known for their tolerance. This country has opened its doors to millions of people from all parts of the world who have made this country a multicultural mosaic where they feel at home, a country that is free in every sense of the word. The Conservative Government has tried several times to change this tradition at some very difficult moments in our history when refugees arrived at our borders without going through the normal process. Granted, in several cases these were phony refugees, but in many cases they were genuine.
Mr. Speaker, it was these circumstances that the Government tried to use in August 1987 to create a so-called national emergency so that it could recall Parliament.

January 28, 1988

If we want to set up a system to stop phony refugees from entering our country, we should realize it is equally important to make sure that genuine refugees can enter this country.
Over that long period of time, Mr, Speaker, the Opposition Parties, as well as various Canadian groups and individuals have begged the Minister of Immigration and this Tory Government to amend Bill C-84 in an effort to uphold this great Canadian tradition of tolerance, to maintain our great open door policy for genuine immigrants and to preserve our reputation as a tolerant country where all citizens of the world who fear for their lives can find here a secure heaven. This way we could continue to show leadership and thus urge all the other countries of the world to hold an international conference, thereby making sure that all those who are persecuted everywhere in the world would not give up hope of coming to a country such as Canada.
Mr. Speaker, of course there are abuses. As in any society, there are abuses: abuses of the unemployment insurance scheme, abuses of the income tax legislation, abuses of the Transport Act. Abuses are everywhere. We are all human and there are people who will take advantage of the system. It is indeed our responsibility, as Parliamentarians, to try to improve our system, to do the utmost to limit the number of possible abuses. But the fact that there are abuses does not justify closing all doors and adopting legislation which is not consistent with the traditions and aspirations of Canadians.
When, having adopted Bill C-84, the Parliament of Canada and this Tory Government with its enormous majority sent it to the other place-I mean, the Senate-the Senators decided to fully discharge their constitutional responsibility and to examine this Bill like any other Bill. They heard witnesses who had come from every part of Canada to make sure that this Bill was consistent with our traditions and our Charter of Rights and Freedoms.
After a while which I would describe as short, without delaying unduly the whole process or using delaying tactics not to be accused of filibustering, a charge this Tory Government has made often recently-the Senate sent back this bill to the House with a few reasonable amendments which would make it possible for the Government to correct the deficiencies which existed in the original Bill C-84.

They said this to the Minister: We are proposing a few amendments which we believe are reasonable. subtopic: IMMIGRATION ACT, 1976 MEASURE TO AMEND-CONSIDERATION OF SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we will try to focus on the Bill, but 1 am sure you realize this is quite difficult, since the proposed amendments come from the other place.
Mr. Speaker, I was saying that the purpose of these changes was to amend a Bill that was tabled in the House in August 1987 to cope with a so-called national emergency.
Mr. Speaker, as I said earlier, it is now January 1988, and Canada is facing neither war nor famine, there is no revolution, and at the time all we had was a hundred or so refugees who arrived one morning on the shores of Nova Scotia.
To get back to the amendments, Mr. Speaker, I would like to discuss the matter of ships whether the Minister has the power to turn back ships. Of course, last summer, at one time the Minister spread rumours that there were boatloads of refugees coming to Canada. Those rumours proved to be no more than that.
So I wonder how we are going to board all ships approaching Canadian shores and make sure everybody on board has a
January 28, 1988

passport and the right papers. Wouldn't it be more convenient, once a ship arrives in a Canadian port, to have legislation so that if there are refugees on board we can take legal steps, confiscate the ship, put the captain in prison, all of which would act as a deterrent to others. On the other hand, if a ship is prevented from entering Canadian waters or a Canadian port, what is going to prevent it from doing what happened this summer, when the ship's captain put his refugees ashore in small boats, at night while no one was looking? In that case, will the Canadian Government at least consider increasing very substantially the surveillance of its shores?
Mr. Speaker, I think the amendments are reasonable. I think the Government and the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Bouchard) could have accepted these amendments and thus have a piece of legislation that would reflect Canadian tradition and conform to the Charter of Rights and Freedoms. However, although the Minister accepted a few amendments because he really had no choice, he said no to all the others because they allegedly changed the substance of the Bill and he could therefore not accept them.

Therefore, we cannot support the action of the Minister in refusing these amendments. We believe that the amendments were necessary in order to keep the Canadian tradition of tolerance and to open our border to those who are in danger.
Yes, there are abuses. There are abuses in the immigration law, there are abuses in the tax law, there are abuses in the transportation laws and there are abuses in the environment laws. So what? Do we arrest everyone? Do we reject completely the unemployment insurance system because some have abused it, or do we try to improve the system and ensure that no one abuses it or that those who abuse it can be prosecuted in a fair and legal way? That is what the other place is trying to tell us. It is not filibustering anything. It is trying to ensure that we in this House pass a Bill that reflects the Canadian tradition and our Charter of Rights and Freedoms.
The Government has accepted some more minor and technical recommendations. This has signalled a recognition on its part that the Bill was overkill. The flexibility proves it erred in drafting the Bill and has vindicated the position we have articulated throughout the debate on Bill C-84. That was not only our position but it was the position of many Canadian groups, churches, unions and people who every day work with refugees.
Let me touch on another point that was part of these amendments which were rejected by the Minister. Let me give the House an example of what sometimes happens to us in our role as Members of Parliament. What will we do if one day someone knocks at the door of my riding office and is desperate, telling me that his life is in danger? Am I to ask him for proof that his life is in danger? I would look at the person and say that I think he is telling the truth and would decide to help the person get refugee status.
Immigration Act, 1976
If, after investigating all the facts, the Immigration Department finds that that person was not telling the truth, am I to go to jail because I helped someone in need, believing and trusting that person who, I thought, was telling the truth? Is that not the Canadian tradition? Is that not what Canada is all about?
Why do we have to close all the doors? If, in 1968 when I came to Canada, the doors had been closed, I would not be here. Perhaps my colleague would not be here and maybe your parents would not be here, Mr. Speaker. Canada would not be the same. Why are we changing something that is so fundamental to Canadian life? That is what we have been telling the Government since August when the Government called Parliament back by saying that there was an emergency. Since then, we have been debating it, and now even the other place is.
Regardless of what government Members or members of the NDP say about the other place, I think it is very reasonable and sensible. They gave us a message. They tried to tell us not to make mistakes and change the Canadian way. I say, let us make those amendments to the Bill and we are going to have a law that reflects and represents Canadian aspirations, Canadian traditions, the Canadian way, and then our kids for generations to come can be proud.

Mr. Speaker, I have about three minutes left. It is important that we as Canadians continue the tradition of our predecessors and show other countries that Canada is a just and free country, and that when a person arrives at our borders and is telling the truth and says that he needs help and needs a place to live, he should be allowed to stay. Since there are people who take advantage of the situation and are trafficking in refugees or abusing the system, we should have legislation that provides for severe penalties in those cases, Mr. Speaker. However, penalizing someone who was acting in good faith to save someone else's life is certainly not the right way. It is not the Canadian way, to let a person who just wanted to help save another human being's life be penalized because that other person abused the system and did not tell the truth. I think the person who failed to tell the truth should be penalized, not the person who was trying to help him. I think that is a very fundamental point, Mr. Speaker. This is part of our Canadian tradition and should remain so.
Mir. Marchi: Mr. Speaker, I was listening carefully to the speech by my colleague, the Hon. Member for Saint-Leon-ard-Anjou (Mr. Gagliano). He spoke very eloquently and I may say very emotionally about the subject of immigration and refugees.
I would like to ask one question of my colleague and it concerns the question he raised in his speech, namely the legal implications of this legislation. One of the overriding, if not the

January 28, 1988
Immigration Act, 1976
overriding, responsibilities of this Chamber and its Members is to draft legislation in keeping with the Constitution, which is our basic law, and the Charter of Rights and Freedoms. We have been told by virtually every legal expert who appeared before the legislative committee dealing with this Bill that it is so seriously flawed that as soon as it hits the books every lawyer worth his or her salt will be challenging it in the courts. It was the same story in the Senate committee. Many of those experts predicted that the court would agree that it is flawed.
That sets up the possibility of a very dangerous situation developing. The Government is conducting a public relations campaign to try to convince Canadians that somehow this legislation will take care of all our problems. The Government is saying not to worry, from this day forward our problems with the refugee determination system will be cured. What, then, is the Government going to do if a court strikes this legislation down because it violates the Charter? That will obviously paralyze the policy and again throw it into chaos.
Could the Hon. Member perhaps share with this House his thoughts on what that will do to the confidence of Canadians in the law, as well as causing increasing frustration and anger among people who have been misled into believing that the problem was solved only to find it worse than before?

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 want to thank my colleague for reminding me of this aspect of the legislation and the overall public relations framework the Government has been building since last summer. You will recall that we were called back in the middle of the summer recess because there was a national emergency. One morning we found around 170 refugees on the Nova Scotia coast. Years back we received thousands of refugees and there was no emergency, but the Government is trying to convince Canadians that there is an emergency now. It said there was something drastically wrong with our system and the only way to solve it was to call Parliament back to deal with this Bill, which gave the false hope that it would solve all the problems. Yes, our immigration and refugee policy needs to be amended, but not in this fashion.
I agree with my hon. colleague that the possibilities are very high that this legislation will be challenged in the court, so that this exercise is useless. We go back to the beginning and those people who should be penalized, those people who take advantage of the system, those people who charge a fee to bring in false refugees, will increase their activities and we will be in a worse situation than we were last summer.
Therefore, I agree with my colleague that the amendments proposed by the other place should be accepted so that this legislation is at least in accordance with our Constitution and Charter of Rights and Freedoms. It can then be put in place and we hope the Government will continue to look at our
refugee policy so that Canada can continue its traditions, which are very well accepted by the rest of the world.

subtopic: IMMIGRATION ACT, 1976 MEASURE TO AMEND-CONSIDERATION OF SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Member for Saint-Leon-ard-Anjou (Mr. Gagliano) quite correctly pointed out the false hope which this administration was trying to generate by trying to fabricate and create a crisis which only existed in the wild imagination of the people on the other side. A measure of that false hope can be seen in the changes which the Government has made in response to the report from the other place. That is to say, even though those changes are to the more minor aspects of the legislation, the Government still made changes which it was not prepared to make last summer.
After a few months had passed and government Members had an opportunity to reflect on what they had done, 1 think they recognized that they had erred and that the legislation was overkill. I would like to commend the Member for Saint-Leonard-Anjou for his observations.
The other aspect was that of creating a new offence for religious institutions, other organizations, and individual Canadians who help with refugees who may not have documents to come to this country. I find that very offensive. Could the Member go into some detail on what he thinks about this particular aspect upon which he touched very briefly?

speechtext: I will allow a very short response by the Hon. Member for Saint-Leonard- Anjou (Mr. Gagliano).

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if before a refugee comes into Canada he has to wait to ensure that he has all the documents to prove he is a genuine refugee, I do not think he will ever make it to Canada. Therefore, it is important that our system allow refugees to come to Canada so that they can be safe, and we can then verify whether they are genuine refugees.
With this legislation we will close all the doors. We will even tell boats not to come near us, to get away because they are not allowed to come. I do not know what measures we will use to accomplish that. Is the Minister going to call in the Army to start shooting? We shall see. Let us hope that we never go that far. This is how ridiculous this thing is getting. It is paranoia. Let us allow any refugee who comes here to come in. We can check them and if they are real refugees they will be welcome because that is our tradition and policy. If they are not genuine refugees they should be looked after and we will ensure that those who profited from bringing them here are penalized. Instead of turning the boat away we should confiscate the boat, arrest the captain, and ensure that the next captains know about it so that they will not take the risk of losing their ships.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to take a few minutes to deal with the legislation put forward by the Hon. Member for Roberval (Mr. Bouchard), the Minister for Employment and Immigration, which legislation is aimed primarily at stopping the massive entry of bogus refugees into this country. As you know, faced with repeated instances of refugee groups coming to this country, we had to recall in August 1987 the House of Commons in order to prepare our legislation aimed at stopping human traffickers, those who offered for financial gain to bring people into Canada, to have them enter illegally. A stop had to be put to that kind of traffic with an aim, first to protect their victims, second to ensure a greater degree of security to Canadians and to protect
Immigration Act, 1976
the interests of Canadian taxpayers who for all practical purposes foot the bill each time there is a massive influx of people by sea or air.
That whole legislation was prepared with a view to maintaining a hospitable climate for legitimate refugees and people who want to enter Canada in order to later live here legally. Those considerations are an integral part of the legislation.
Our proposal received massive support from the people- there were only a few objections.
The opposition comes mainly from the coalition, what we now call the Liberal-Socialist coalition, a coalition described by the Leader of the Liberal Party (Mr. Turner), because they claim that at the next election, if there is a coalition of people from the left, this will help sink us lower into debt, as those people from the left did during the last 20 years under Liberal rule.
We therefore face an opposition from a coalition of Liberals in partnership with their Socialist comrades. Those people always refused to support the introduction of our Bill to the Senate.
We introduced it recently to the Senate, and it came back. Because in the Senate they also decided to oppose democracy.
Some 120 years ago, Mr. Speaker, this Chamber was given authority to legislate. And since last year the Senate, which is dominated by Liberals, Grits, friends of the former Prime Minister-perhaps enemies of the current Leader of the Opposition-has increasingly opposed legislation from the House of Commons, defying the Canadian Constitution, defying democracy. Curiously, the Senate should be the keeper of democracy-
So, they opposed our legislation, they sent it back. As they did when we proposed Bill C-22 concerning the Drugs Act. It was a non-ending struggle against the Senate. Liberal senators travelled across Canada, as they did with this legislation, in order to listen to Canadians, to hear them repeat the same things. Canadians agreed with Bill C-22, but the Senate, supported by the Liberal caucus-and I see that some members of the Liberal caucus are here now-defied the House of Commons on Bill C-22 and continues to defy it on Bill C-84, with the support of some of the Members from Quebec. For instance, the Hon. Member for Laval-des-Rapides (Mr. Garneau) was quite happy to delay passage of Bill C-22, which could create thousands of jobs in the Montreal region.
Mr. Speaker, it is important to expedite passage of this Bill because there are now 30,000 claims for refugee status in Canada. In 1987, 30,000 applications were made. We have to speed up the processing of these claims, but to do so, the Members of the Liberal-socialist coalition must help us move matters forward, and it is especially important for the Liberal caucus and its questioned and questionable Leader to advise Members opposite of the urgency of this legislation. There are

still two parties in the Opposition; the coalition is not a fact yet.
It would also be appropriate to tell the public about the position of the socialist party as concerns this Bill. Their lack of interest is obvious as there are not very many of them in the House to discuss this Bill. However, what is their position? What have they been saying?

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, any Bill which deals with immigration or refugees, brought in by any Government whatsoever, would have to lead to very vigorous debate and discussion because the people of Canada are as divided on these questions as they are on any question. It is not surprising when we have over a million Canadians unemployed that many Canadians believe we have permitted too many immigrants to come into this country. They believe this has resulted to a large extent in this unemployment problem. Those people who believe that will not listen or pay attention to any study-and many have been done-which indicates that immigrants bring more benefits to the country than difficulties and that immigration has not been a factor with respect to the large number of unemployed in Canada. There are people, such as the former Chief Justice of the Supreme Court of British Columbia, and a former senior official in the Department of Immigration, who opposed the legislation we passed in the 1960s and the present legislation because, under the provisions of the legislation, under the regulations, a substantial number of people have come to Canada as immigrants or refugees who are non-white and these people believe, and I completely reject their belief, that we ought to maintain our white civilization, as they call it.
I am not surprised we have a great deal of debate, some of it pretty emotional, any time we talk about changing our immigration laws. Let us get the record clear. The Bill brought forward by this Government months ago has been thoroughly analysed, discussed and debated by thousands of Canadians. The fact is that many organizations representing millions of Canadians expressed their opposition to the provisions of this Bill and to its objectives when the Bill was first introduced, and they expressed those same objections when the Bill was being discussed and debated in the Senate. They approved in the main the amendments moved in the Senate which were rejected almost entirely by the Government. As I said on an earlier occasion, I have never in my 25 years as a Member of

January 28, 1988
Immigration Act, 1976
Parliament seen such a unanimous reaction and opposition to this Bill as we have seen in the last year. Let me put on the record the names of some of the organizations which have expressed their opposition to this Bill.
The organizations include the Canadian Ethnocultural Council, which represents most of the ethnic groups and peoples in this country, the Canadian Bar Association, the Canadian Jewish Congress, the Canadian Labour Council, and the Canadian Council of Churches, which takes in the major non-Catholic churches. Included among these are the Anglican church, the United church, the Presbyterian church, the Mennonite Central Committee, the Salvation Army, the Quakers and the Baptists. We have the World Relief Canada which acts on behalf of 23 of the evangelical Protestant denominations. Last but not least, and I wish the Hon. Member who spoke a few moments ago were still here, we have the Canadian Conference of Catholic Bishops. To suggest that these organizations-which are almost all, if not all, nonpolitical-are part of some kind of Liberal-socialist coalition, and participating, therefore, for partisan political reasons, is, of course, so ludicrous that one wonders why any Member would make such a suggestion.
It is not that they want anyone to be permitted to come into this country as a refugee. They recognize, as everyone does, that there is no way in which any Government in Canada, regardless of its political persuasion, could permit all the people who want to come to Canada as immigrants or refugees to do so.
This is one of the best countries in the world in which to live. We have one of the highest standards of living. We are one of the most democratic countries in the world. Of course, people from nearly every country in the world would like to come to live in Canada. Of course, no Government could permit everyone who wants to come here to do so. We know, and these organizations which oppose this particular piece of legislation know, that there are many people who come to Canada claiming refugee status who are in fact not refugees but who come here for economic or other reasons.
We know that any Government would have to pass legislation which would permit sensible screening and inquiry with respect to the application. However, that is not what this Bill does. This Bill ignores the recommendations made by the organizations which I have listed. It ignores the recommendations made by Rabbi Gunther Plaut, who was appointed by the former Liberal Government to do a study of the whole question of refugees and how we should deal with their applications. He tabled his report after the Conservative Government took office. He made a number of very sound and sensible, humanitarian proposals. The Standing Committee on Employment and Immigration held a whole series of hearings. That committee, as every committee of this House, included a substantial majority of Conservatives. They made a number of very good recommendations. Those recommendations were almost entirely ignored by the Government in the drafting of the Bill.
The United Nations High Commission for Refugees has said that this Bill violates our agreement with the United Nations with respect to how we deal with refugees. The Government has demonstrated conclusively that it does not have a policy which is based on any kind of principles. The best illustration of that fact is how the Government dealt with two groups of people who claimed refugee status in very similar circumstances.
The first case involved the case of the Tamils who arrived by boat on the coast of Nova Scotia and who claimed refugee status. They were welcomed by the Government of Canada. They were assured by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) that they would be treated in a friendly way. The assumption was made, very properly, that they would be granted refugee status.
One year later another similar group of over 100 Sikhs under similar circumstances arrived on the shores of Nova Scotia. This time they were given the cold shoulder. We were told that they were not genuine refugees and that they would not be granted refugee status quickly and easily. Why? They were in the same circumstance as was the earlier group. The Government listened to what it thought was the feelings of Canadians. It came to the conclusion that the Canadian people had had enough and that they wanted to get tough with so-called refugees. The Government felt that Canadians did not want to let these people in. Thus the Government changed its position and brought in this legislation.
Groups which have opposed this type of legislation have made it clear that they want the Government to deal with refugee claimants fairly, humanely, honestly and expeditiously. They have not said that every person who claims that he or she is a refugee should be permitted to stay in Canada. The Government has demonstrated its inability not only to adopt the policy based on any principle but to deal with cases which arise quickly, fairly and expeditiously.
I remind Hon. Members that several years ago there were hundreds of Portuguese flying into Canada claiming refugee status. They claimed that they were Jehovah's Witnesses and as such were being persecuted and prosecuted in Portugal. That was obviously and patently untrue. It took the Government months before it made a simple decision which would have stopped such nonsense. All it had to do was to put in place a regulation stating that people wishing to come from Portugal had to have a visa, one which they could obtain from the Canadian Embassy in Portugal. The Government did not do that.
A similar situation occurred when hundreds of people came to Canada from Turkey claiming that they were being prosecuted and persecuted. This occurred at a time when Turkey was moving to a more democratic system of Government. They did not appear in Canada when Turkey was under military rule, when people were being arrested, imprisoned and
January 28, 1988

worse. Again, the Government took forever before it insisted that people coming to Canada from Turkey had to have a visa.
The Government has demonstrated that it does not know what to do and how to deal with refugees. It has failed to do it and continues to fail to do it. As I indicated to my friend in the case of the terrorist, of course, he cannot be a genuine refugee. Of course he cannot be permitted to stay in Canada, because he was involved in a terrorist activity. He was arrested. He was charged. He was tried and convicted. He was sentenced. He served time in prison. He hid all of this from the Canadian authorities in the Department of Immigration and officers in the security service when he was asked to give information about his record. It is obvious that the Government in bringing forward this Bill has brought forward a Bill which is deficient in most of its major provisions.
What should there be in this Bill? What is wrong with it? There is no provision for any meaningful appeal process. Given the decision that the Supreme Court of Canada made today on the question of abortion, and although I am not a lawyer, I am certain that if and when this Bill passes there will be appeals to the courts by people who wish to be granted refugee status because there are provisions in the Bill which violate the provisions of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms which is now part of the Constitution. This is something with which the Canadian Bar Association agrees.
There is no provision in the Bill for humanitarian or compassionate cases, something that exists in the present Act. This Bill puts emphasis on whether the applicant for refugee status stopped in a safe third country. What that means is that we in this independent country of Canada will permit to an alarming extent the type of decisions we make was to be made by another country.
There are thousands of people who are in the United States as refugees who have come from Chile or some of the Central American countries such as El Salvador, Nicaragua or other countries with respect to which the American Government refuses to recognize refugees under its laws. Since those people have moved from the country where they used to live to the United States, which is a safe third country, when they come to our country under the provisions of this Bill they could be denied refugee status. This is so not because they are refugees coming from the countries which they have left because of political persecution or other reasons but because they were already in the United States, which is a safe third country.
I wish to tell Hon. Members that in the United States members of a number of churches, including the Roman Catholic Church and the Mennonites, who have been involved in helping these refugees whom the United States consider to be illegal have been charged with offences under American law as interpreted by the Reagan administration. They have been taken to court and found guilty of aiding people who are illegally in the country. If this Bill is passed, it will mean that Canada could be co-operating with that type of action which is
Immigration Act, 1976
being taken by the United States. I want to tell Hon. Members that I certainly intend to have no part in that kind of situation.
Let me conclude by saying what I indicated earlier. The Government has rejected many of the proposals of the parliamentary committee which dealt with this question. As I also indicated earlier, a majority of the members of the committee were Conservative Members. They proposed in their report that there should be a swift and fair system of refugee status determination. They also proposed that a refugee claimant should be sent directly to the refugee board without a lot of immigration procedures, and that the board could decide on that status having been trained and authorized to do so. The Immigration Department could take over from there and either admit the person on refugee grounds or, if there are no other humanitarian grounds, expel the person from the country. According to the committee, that would have required only four months, not the years it presently takes. The Government rejected that.
Members of the committee suggested that there should be an immigration adjudicator who would be a member of the refugee division, to examine the eligibility and credibility of the claimant. That person would not judge the merits of his or claim, but only whether he or she could be safe in another country through which he or she passed and should be removed to that country, or whether the country from which the claimant is fleeing is in fact one which does not produce refugees. That suggestion was rejected by the Government, as were almost all others.
When the Bill went to the Senate, hearings were held on it. With the exception of representatives of the Department and the Government, I understand that virtually all other submissions by witnesses as individuals or organizations pointed out the faults in the Bill and called for amendments, which were approved in the main by the Senate. Some of the most responsible organizations in the country, including the churches, the Labour Congress, and the Canadian Bar Association, have called for those amendments. As I have indicated, those suggestions embodied in the amendments have almost entirely been rejected by the Government.
I want to say again, as have other members of the New Democratic Party, that we opposed the original Bill and that we continue to oppose what is contained in the present motion.
Mir. Blaikie: I should like to make a comment, Mr. Speaker. One thing which amazed me about the Government's response to the criticism of this Bill has been its complete unwillingness to admit the unjustified nature of putting a great many church people in the situation in which it is going to put them by passing this legislation. It makes no distinction, as I understand it, between those who aid and abet or help someone, who they believe is a legitimate refugee but may not have the appropriate documents, and people who, for money or for other less justifiable reasons, knowingly bring people into the

January 28, 1988
Business of the House
country who do not have documents without any conviction that they are legitimate refugees. The Government has not made that kind of distinction. It did not make it when it first brought in the legislation.
It has, for reasons which are completely mysterious to me, resisted any attempts to clarify the legislation in a way which would make it possible for a great many otherwise law-abiding, decent Canadians, most of whom are active in one Canadian church or another, to work actively within a network that sometimes extends through the church all the way down to Central America, for instance, and to help people who are legitimate refugees get into the country. They do not smuggle in these people in that sense. They do not do anything clandestine. As soon as a person comes to this country, they take that person without documents directly to the nearest immigration office and say: "We have reason to believe that this person has a legitimate refugee claim". Everything is above board and everything is on the table, yet these people are to be classified as criminals under this legislation.
For the life of me I cannot understand why the Government will not make a distinction between those kinds of people and the people who everyone agrees should be curbed by the law, people who are organizing one scam or another for getting people into the country who do not have, and no one believes to have, a legitimate claim to being a refugee.
I do not know whether the Government is planning some kind of persecution of the churches in Canada. One starts to wonder after a while just what is coming down the road, the Minister says that that is not what they have in mind and that they would not do that sort of thing. If that is so, then why not clarify the legislation so that it would not be possible for them to do it? I just do not understand.
I think it is one of the more reprehensible aspects of this Bill alongside its reprehensibility in respect of the way it treats the human rights of refugees.

Mr. Speaker, in examining this issue, 1 am very happy that my colleague, the Hon. Member for York West (Mr. Marchi), is here. From the perspective of the Liberal Party he has been leading the fight.
In an analysis of what I have to say, even after the amendments that have been accepted by the Government, Bill C-84 is a very bad Bill. 1 think we have to look at the political context. If we recall last summer, some of us were working in Hamilton on a by-election and others were lounging on beaches across the country or enjoying their vacations with their families when we were called back to Parliament allegedly to deal with an emergency issue. It was an emergency issue that in my estimation the Government trumped up in response to a situation which saw a number of refugees coming to Canada by boat. Rather than following the recommendations of the refugee study that had been conducted by Rabbi Gunther Plaut, the Government chose to ignore the whole issue during the three first years of its mandate and then, all of a sudden, came forward with emergency legislation in late summer which was supposed to deal with an emergency situation. It was so urgent that the Bill dragged on and on and the Government did not move ahead as quickly as it said it would.
In the meantime, what we have seen is certainly a great degree of public concern about some of the policies that touch immigration in Canada. I think those are valid concerns. But unfortunately I believe the Conservative Government has been exploiting those legitimate concerns of Canadians about having a fair and equitable system. It has been mixing apples and oranges, if I can use the analogy. The Government has been mixing apples and oranges because it has been reaching out claiming somehow that the opposition Parties have been delaying passage of legislation which would improve the situation.

speechtext:
In fact, what we have been trying to do is to continue the long tradition that we have in Canada of reasonable laws to deal with immigration in an open way and to deal with refugees in a sympathetic way and in a manner which has been historical in our country.
You will recall that Canada is the only country that as a nation has been recognized internationally for its contribution to those people who fled from Vietnam by boat, the so-called boat people. We were recognized internationally because, among all other nations, we reached out from our pocket books, as church groups and from our hearts as individuals and
Immigration Act, 1976
decided to mount a massive campaign assisted by the Government to permit legitimate refugees to settle in Canada. We have had a long and proud tradition of accepting not only immigrants who come to Canada through the normal application process, applying from their native countries, but we have also had a long and cherished tradition of accepting the stateless, the homeless and people who have nowhere else to do. I think this is a tradition we want to continue. That is why we cannot support the Bill currently before the House in the terms of Bill C-84.
There are two major flaws to Bill C-84. I think it is important we discuss them. At first blush I do not think the public, not even the politicians, always understand the nuances of the difference between an immigration policy and a refugee policy. In my own riding I spent a lot of time trying to assist people who would like to bring relatives from other countries. They look at people who come by boat and say, "Hey, this person is somehow getting ahead of me. He is jumping the queue. He should wait, stand in line and take his turn". But we know quite clearly that there are two streams for entry into Canada. One is the immigration process. Every year, through the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Bouchard), a number is established for immigrants who want to come to Canada from other countries. I personally believe that the number we establish generally is far too low. My friend the critic from the riding of York West may correct me but I believe on average we usually accept somewhere in the neighbourhood of about 200,000 people who emigrate from other countries. In my own case I was privileged to be able to sponsor a spouse from another country. That is the process that we have in place for general immigration and for family reunification. These are objectives that should be lauded.
On the other hand we have always recognized as a people that there are difficult political situations and different kinds of immigration solutions. Hence we have established a process to permit refugees to come to Canada in a way that is different from the way in which we assist the normal immigration process. For example, if you are required to flee your country with only the shirt on your back to save your life you cannot always apply with the proper documentation. I have friends in Hamilton who fled from Vietnam and I was involved with a group who sponsored them. They came to Canada with only the shirts on their backs. They literally left Vietnam in the dead of night, escaping a rule that was not acceptable to them, and they came to Canada and were accepted as refugees. They did move ahead of the normal immigration process because they did not have a homeland. They were stateless people, floating around in a boat.
While, on the one hand, you could argue that we should assist the Government in its objective to make sure that people who come to Canada and claim refugee status are legitimate refugees, but, on the other hand, how can we allow that process to be established if we pass a law which says we will turn the boat away?

Let us examine that for a moment, Mr. Speaker. You will remember this very sad story in the Second World War of the boat full of Jewish refugees that went from port to port and country to country getting turned away at every place. Hopefully, as Canadians, when we turned that boatload of Jewish refugees away, we learned a lesson. We said that in the future if a person or a group of people come to our shores and wanted to claim refugee status, we owed them the responsibility of due process.
If we turn a boat away, which is the intention of the Government's amendment, in violation of U.N. conventions, not only are we denying due process but we are assisting the very people whom, we claim, we want to put out of business. If I were the captain of a boat, a mercenary, and I wanted to drop a boatload of refugees or alleged refugees off the shores of Canada and I knew Canadians would turn the boat away, I would drop the people off farther offshore so that I was not in Canadian waters and I would get away with it. Captains of boats are receiving cash on demand, payable in advance. The boat owner is often running, probably having skimmed millions of dollars from refugees or would-be refugees who have sought passage on the boat, and is scot-free in another country merely because he drops refugees outside the 200 mile limit. The refugees or would-be refugees may drown, they may reach our shores and they may be dealt with in the due process at that time.
We are suggesting what we think is a more reasonable amendment, that would be, to throw the owner in jail, seize the boat and dispose of its assets for the Crown. That will make the boat owner realize that he cannot rip off would-be refugees and exploit the poor and homeless. That is why we are proposing these amendments.
I realize that my time is up so I will resume tomorrow.

speechtext:
that Bill C-264, an Act to amend the Criminal Code (instruments and literature for illicit drug use) be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I am here this afternoon to begin debate on second reading of what I feel is a very important Bill which I introduced for first reading on September 14, 1987. I do not have to tell you about the problem that exists in Canada, Mr. Speaker. I know that you as a long time Member of the House know that there is a very, very serious drug abuse problem in Canada, a problem which affects all Canadians but mainly young Canadians. It is the young Canadians I am trying to protect by bringing in this Bill.
This problem has been discussed many times in the House in recent months. I do not think that any one of the 282 Members of the House would refute its importance. We all know the social and economic cost of drug abuse. 1 could quote reams and reams of statistics showing that drug use is on the rise. Drug seizures by police forces in Canada measured in kilograms show that in 1981, 38.528 kilograms of cocaine were seized. In 1986, that figure was 102.686. In 1981, 7.154 kilograms of heroin were seized, and in 1986, the figure was 44.482. It is on the rise and we know that. We are facing a very, very serious problem.
Many people have studied this problem. The Health and Welfare Committee studied it at length and came to certain conclusions and recommendations. I think it is time some action was taken on them.
As a Member of Parliament, and I think 1 am fairly typical, 1 have commiserated with parents of young people who were in foreign jails for attempting to smuggle cocaine. I have talked with them and tried to console them. I have tried to arrange consular visits. Recently I was with the Justice Committee in Kingston and spoke with a young woman in the women's penitentiary there. She was 35 years of age and told me that she started on drugs when she was 15 and had been an addict since. It had led her to the women's penitentiary. She cried when she spoke to me.
I do not think there is anyone in the House who does not know of a family in his or her community who has been touched by drug abuse. I think that this is the most serious situation we face. How can we expect to be a country that can compete with all other industrialized countries in the world on a free trade basis when our youth are subjected to drugs?
Most of these drugs are cultivated elsewhere and are brought into Canada. There is a constant supply of them. If there is no demand for them, the supply will cease. Sometimes it is very difficult, but if we could educate our children to say no to the supply that constantly exists, brought in by unscrupulous people, the supply would dry up because the demand would not be there. Sometimes, though, adolescents do not have the self-assurance or self-confidence to say no to things like this and therefore become involved.
I would like to tell the House where the inconsistency arises. Everyone knows that cocaine and heroin are illegal substances. At the same time, there are stores across Canada that sell drug paraphernalia. Believe me, there are not just one or two of them but hundreds of them. In Ontario, there are 300 and in
January 28, 1988

Alberta there are 100, There are some in the Yukon and they are moving into the smaller communities as well.
Flow can it be that a substance like cocaine is illegal while at the same time it is perfectly legal to sell drug paraphernalia anywhere in Canada, down on Rideau Street, on Yonge Street in Toronto and in Mississauga, I am sure, although I have not looked? These shops are called head shops by the youth. This comes from the word "pothead". In the 1960s, drug addicts were called potheads.
There are head shops where one can buy all of the drug paraphernalia one needs. We know that cocaine is illegal and that crack is made by mixing cocaine with caustic soda and water and boiling it. I do not know exactly how it is done, but it is a very dangerous drug. It has to be smoked in a pyrex pipe with a screen. These pipes can be purchased in these stores. There are many things including dispensers for cocaine and razor blades that do not fit any razors that are used to line up and mix cocaine. These can be bought anywhere.
Parents Against Drugs was the organization which so effective impressed me with the seriousness of the problem of drug paraphernalia in Canada, and that is what we are here today to debate. This Bill is a very small, concise Bill. It calls for an amendment to the Criminal Code of Canada to prohibit the sale of drug paraphernalia. I believe it is a good Bill.
1 believe that there are shopkeepers who have drug paraphernalia on their shelves who, if they come to realize the heartbreak and misery these paraphernalia bring to the youth of Canada and their parents, will take them off their shelves and will replace them with something else. However, 1 also believe that there are unscrupulous people who do not care if they leave a trail of heartbreak behind them. They are in it for the money. They set up these shops next to video arcades where young people happen to be and they glamorize drug use. They sell products which tell the youth of our nation that drugs are the greatest thing that ever happened and that without drugs they cannot get along. These shops must be closed.
If I may, I would like to refer to the testimony of Assistant Commissioner Heaton of the RCMP before a Standing Committee of this House. He said:
1 think if we are really serious about the drug problem, there is probably no better place to start than to look at the drug paraphernalia. At a time when we put forth preventive education of our young people as a priority, there is an industry that thrives in this country delivering a completely contradictory message. We permit retail outlets that are called "head shops" to operate, and they distribute literature, equipment, and material to facilitate and enhance the use of illicit drugs. The paradox of such an industry is all too obvious. It relies on the message of drugs and their glamour for youth, and it delivers a message that really is directly opposite to what needs to be taught.
I do not think anyone in this House objects to closing these shops. Every one of the 282 Members must know that if we are going to combat drug abuse effectively we must get on with it.

We have had calls for the banning of head shops by witnesses from the RCMP, the Canadian Association of Chiefs of Police, the Ontario Association of Chiefs of Police, Alcohol and Drug Concerns Inc., Parents Against Drug Abuse, the Ontario Secondary School Principals Council, the Ontario Association of Home and School Associations, Youth Alcohol and Drug Community Action, and many others. I believe this is something the Government must do during this mandate.
I would like to pay special tribute to Mrs. Joan Gitterman of Parents Against Drugs who wrote me a letter asking me to become involved. I have spoken at banquets and meetings of that organization and, believe me, I think every Member of this House should vote in favour of this amendment to the Criminal Code.
The Bill is only two pages and I will read the explanatory note:
The purpose of this Bill is to prohibit commerce in illicit drug paraphernalia.
At present, although narcotics and certain drugs are outlawed, literature
glamorizing their use and devices and kits facilitating it are freely available in
so-called "head shops" and elsewhere.
If an addict came to a town and did not know where to get a drug supply, where would be the obvious place to go? I think he would go to a head shop where he would be directed to where he could get a supply of the drugs he needs.
We have in Canada today an outrageous number of addicts. In Alberta, the province you represent, Mr. Speaker, there are over 2,000 heroin addicts alone. There are over 2,000 in Metropolitan Toronto. These lives are being wasted. These are people Canada needs and I would hate to see any more of our youth brought to the use and abuse of drugs because of these head shops. I call on every Member of this House to stand in his or her place and vote with me to bring about the abolition of the sale of drug paraphernalia and thereby cut down on drug abuse in this country.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Bill C-264, introduced by my friend the Hon. Member for Mississauga North (Mr. Horner), addresses an issue which is both important and delicate. The purpose of this bill is to prohibit commerce in illicite drugs paraphernalia. At present, although narcotics and certain drugs are outlawed, literature glamorizing their use and devices and kits facilitating it are freely available in so-called "head shops" and elsewhere. 1 intend to deal quickly with the problem of drug abuse in Canada as well as those connected with the sale of drug paraphernalia. First of all, I want to congragulate the Hon. Member for his interest in this matter. All those presents realize the importance of the drug abuse problem in Canada.
I certainly feel very strongly about the drug abuse problem in Canada. Such recent events as the announcement by the Government of a national strategy against drugs have caused me and many Canadian people to ponder the general issue of drug abuse.

January 28, 1988
Illicit Drugs Promotion
We are aware that the drug abuse problem in Canada is both complex and old; it includes the use of illicit drugs as well as the uncontrolled consumption of alcohol and prescription drugs. The social cost of drug abuse on individuals is enormous. The detrimental effects of drug abuse on individuals, families and communities through highway accidents causing injuries and death, and threaten the security of the work place.
I will emphasize that over the past years, the most monstrous and frightening crimes were commited following the use of drugs.
Concerning illicit drugs, we know that a great many Canadians are using them socially. This habit has taken such proportions, especially among the young people of high school and college age, that the use of some of these drugs, especially marijuana, is almost part of the social mores.
The number of users has increased in spite of two decades of severe penalties, a strict enforcement of the legislation and increased police powers. This has brought many people to conclude that current legislation have been unable to discourage the use of drugs. The present penal system, as established under the Narcotic Control Act as well as the Food and Drug Act, prohibits the use, distribution and production of narcotics, controlled drugs and restricted drugs.
All offences created by those statutes are indictable offences or hybrid offences, that is offences that could be prosecuted by way of indictment or by way of summary conviction.
The penalties are very serious and include a maximum seven-year imprisonment for drug possession, life imprisonment for drug trafficking and possession for trafficking purposes and a maximum seven-year imprisonment for growing common opium poppy or marijuana, that is cannabis.
Aware of the problem, the federal Government announced in May last year a five-year action plan against drug abuse that involves $210 million. The federal plan will bring new resources to fund initiatives in the area of public information, treatment and rehabilitation, law enforcement and research at the international, national, provincial and community levels.
The work of police forces and federal and provincial government agencies has not been in vain. We see the trends in illicit drugs usage change. For instance, young people seem to use fewer and fewer illicit drugs. A recent study by the Addiction Research Foundation of Ontario looked at alcohol and drug usage by Ontario teenagers in 1987 and the trends observed in that area since 1977. It considered the consumption habits of 4,267 students of the seventh, ninth, eleventh and thirteenth grades. Researchers have found that consumption had gone down between 1985 and 1987, which confirms the trend first noted in 1979.
The amendments to the Criminal Code proposed by my hon. colleague for Mississauga North (Mr. Horner) are well-intentioned. However, this anti-drug paraphernalia Bill is very vague. It refers to the devices generally, but without describing them or giving a complete list. Such lack of precision would
only cause serious problems to the police officers responsible for enforcing the proposed amendments. I recognize that the battle has not yet been won although there seems to be a downward trend in drug use. We have to remain vigilant as concerns the problem of drug abuse and continue the fight against illicit drugs in accordance with the guidelines of the federal action plan against drug abuse. In this regard, Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Justice (Mr. Hnatyshyn) has announced a review of the whole issue of illicit drug paraphernalia. The results of this review should be known later this year. This is why I believe that consideration of the Bill introduced by my hon. colleague should be delayed until the results of the review being carried out by the Minister of Justice are known.
