Mr. Speaker, I want to compliment the Hon. Member for Mississauga North (Mr. Horner) for presenting this Bill. We all realize, from his speech and from his past interest in this subject, the seriousness with which he presents it. The Member speaks with some authority. He represents one of the biggest urban ridings in Canada and I am sure he has come in contact with many people experiencing this problem which we have, especially in our urban areas. The Member also speaks with authority as a former law enforcement officer. He had a distinguished career with the Royal Canadian Mounted Police.
With all of that in mind, we must take this Bill very seriously. It is not a trivial matter as some people may perceive it. At one time or another we all come in contact with the problems which drug abuse has created in our society. We often perceive it to be a teenage problem, but that is not the case because it is not only teenagers who are involved with drugs today. There are people who are not yet teenagers who get involved with drugs.
As the Hon. Member for Mississauga North pointed out, while head shops do not sell drugs, they certainly give the indication that that is what that paraphernalia will be used for. As he pointed out additionally, while they do not sell drugs, 1 am sure that if you wanted to find out where drugs were sold they would be among the better places to find out. I am not saying that all head shops perform that service, but they are in the business of selling paraphernalia which will be used in the selling and glamorization of drugs.
The Hon. Member for Mississauga North has introduced this Bill to amend the Criminal Code. The purpose of the Bill is to prohibit commerce in illicit drugs paraphernalia. As we all know, although narcotics and certain drugs are prohibited, books and other literature glamorizing the use of these drugs and devices and kits facilitating the use of these drugs are presently freely available in what we call head shops in many of our major urban areas.
January 28, 1988

The introduction of this Bill is very timely. As you know, the issue of drug abuse is a very serious one on which the Government has recently taken a great deal of action. You may recall that not long ago the Government announced its national drug strategy whereby it indicated its very real intent to come to terms with the drug abuse problem in the country. The issue of drug paraphernalia is closely related to the whole problem of drug abuse.
Many of us are aware that several states in the United States have adopted anti-drug paraphernalia legislation. Accordingly, for the next few moments I would like to outline some of the actions that U.S. authorities have taken.
Accessories for drug use include pipes, water-pipes, rolling papers, clips, mirrors, razor blades, and a host of gadgets to aid in the preparation, storage, and consumption of controlled substances. These items first became commercially available on a relatively small scale in the mid-1960s in boutiques and record stores. As the popularity of paraphernalia grew, so did the number of stores that sold them. Some shops began to appear that carried nothing else. These stores in particular came to be known as head shops. There were several thousand of them in the United States in the early 1970s.
While the paraphernalia industry grew, opposition began to be voiced by concerned parents, religious leaders, and government officials. Initially the resistance was weak and much of it disorganized. As long as shops were small and relatively inconspicuous they attracted little attention, but by the 1970s head shops could be found in suburban malls and in respectable neighbourhoods.
The first organized group to oppose the paraphernalia industry emerged in Georgia in 1977 under the name of Dekalb Families in Action. They argued that the entire industry was in conflict with the government policy of controlling drugs and that head shops give young people the impression that drug use is socially acceptable. Similar groups organized in other parts of the country and pressed local Governments for ordinances prohibiting the sale of drug accouterments.
Between 1977 and 1979 many municipalities and three states passed laws prohibiting the possession and distribution of paraphernalia. These first statutes were inevitably struck down as being unconstitutional. In May, 1979, the White House requested that the Department of Justice's Drug Enforcement Agency attempt to develop a constitutionally permissible approach to the control of paraphernalia.
The DEA's response to the White House request was to develop a model drug paraphernalia Act. Hearings were held before the House Select Committee on Narcotics and Drug Abuse control in November, 1979, to review the model Act. The committee concluded its review by finding that the paraphernalia industry contributed to the flagrant and harmful use of drugs and found that the model Act was necessary to eradicate the paraphernalia industry.
Illicit Drugs Promotion
However, it was suggested that the problem of drug paraphernalia would be better addressed by state and local government initiatives. Because many state and local antiparaphernalia laws had been struck down as unconstitutional, the DEA developed the model Act which could then be adopted into the state anti-drug statutes.
I would like to go over some of the basic provisions of the American model Act. First, it provides a comprehensive definition of the term "drug paraphernalia" with specific descriptions of the most common forms of paraphernalia. It outlines the relevant factors a court or other authority should consider in determining whether an object comes within that definition. It makes the manufacturer, advertisement, delivery, or use of drug paraphernalia a criminal offence. It makes the delivery of drug paraphernalia to a minor-that being a person under the age of 18 years-a special offence.
The Act it defines clearly what conduct is prohibited regarding the manufacture, advertisement, delivery, or use of drug paraphernalia and specifies what criminal state of mind must accompany such conduct. It also provides for the civil seizure and forfeiture of drug paraphernalia.
In addition, local Governments in the United States have also taken the initiative by adopting zoning and licensing regulations that bar sales of drug paraphernalia to minors, limiting the type of advertising and display of drug paraphernalia items, and controlling where head shops can be located. Such regulations are similar to those governing pornography shops and adult theatres.
1 will cite some examples of the municipal exercise of this jurisdiction. A Philadelphia ordinance requires zoning board approval to open a head shop within 1,000 feet of a school, church, or library. In Massachusetts there is an ordinance which requires current paraphernalia merchants to be licensed and prevents new stores from offering the merchandise. In Illinois there is an ordinance which makes it unlawful to sell or display paraphernalia in premises in close proximity-that being 1,500 feet-to any public or private school, daycare centre, nursery, church, synagogue or any place of worship, park, or liquor licence seeker.
Alternatively, municipalities in Florida and New Jersey adopted anti-paraphernalia ordinances that include bans against the promotion or advertisement of drug paraphernalia. Given the wide-ranging initiatives that have developed at the local government level in the United States, it is encouraging to note that the Supreme Court of Canada has recently ruled as constitutional a provincial prohibition of nude dancing that was a condition of issuance of a liquor licence. This case would appear to endorse local government initiatives to regulate illicit activities without falling into constitutionally prohibited areas.
1 hope that municipalities across Canada have taken a good look at this decision to assess their competence to deal with the problem of drug paraphernalia merchants. I am sure that the study group that is being created by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Hnatyshyn) will also be looking at this new development.

January 28, 1988
Illicit Drugs Promotion
At the same time as U.S. legislative initiatives were developed, the industry that was involved in the manufacture and distribution of so-called neutral products that could be adopted for use in the ingestion or storage of controlled drugs adopted a responsible position of self regulation. The Suggested Paraphernalia Industry Guidelines stated that smoking-related products and other novelty items should not be advertised or merchandised with any reference or illustration involving: the possible illegal use of the products; any illegal drugs or substances; or claims that the product can increase the strength or effectiveness of illegal drugs or substances.
The retail seller of smoking-related products and other novelty items should: post signs prominently indicating "smoking-related items not sold to minors"; require proper identification if a customer's age is in question; instruct sales personnel that customer requests for specific illegal products such as hash pipes, marijuana rolling papers, cocaine spoons, should be courteously turned aside while indicating that pipes, rolling papers and other novelty items are available.
This is a short review of the experience that our neighbours to the south have had. It is clear that the road to creation of legislative responses to the problem of drug paraphernalia has not been smooth. Given the extent to which American constitutional jurisprudence is being accepted in Canadian courts, it is appropriate to review their initiatives and judicial responses.
1 want to compliment the Member for Mississauga North for bringing this to our attention in the Chamber. 1 hope the Government takes his initiatives seriously. All of us realize that there is a problem and I emphasize again that these head shops are there for only one purpose. We know why they exist and, as far as I am concerned, it is time the Government took a serious look at the Hon. Member's Bill, and, if not pass it, do something in this particular area.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-BILLS   CRIMINAL CODE MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is indeed due to the work of a thoughtful and concerned Member that this Private Members' Bill is introduced dealing with the paraphernalia used in the consumption of illicit drugs. I want to congratulate him for his foresight.
1 am pleased to have the opportunity to speak in support of the Member for Mississauga North (Mr. Horner) who has introduced this amendment to the Criminal Code. The purpose of this Bill is to prohibit the sale of drug-related paraphernalia.
Presently, the sale of such material is not prohibited by any specific provision of the Criminal Code, Food and Drugs Act or Narcotic Control Act even though the sale, possession and use of illicit drugs is clearly prohibited.
This obviously leads to a perceived contradiction relating to the federal Government's approach to the drug problem. On the one hand, illicit drugs are rigorously controlled by law, while on the other hand, the accessories used to consume or
otherwise ingest these drugs are being allowed to be openly marketed in stores across Canada. 1 believe that is a frightening situation and, accordingly, I am very sympathetic with the underlying motives of my colleague in introducing this Bill.
1 want to take a few moments to discuss the broad problem of drug paraphernalia and the drug problem on the whole.
During the past 50 years public pressure to control drug abuse has waxed and waned. In the 1960s and 1970s, marijuana use appeared to receive a degree of acceptance in some quarters. Later, cocaine took on an unprecedented fashionabil-ity, again in some quarters. While heroin continued to be feared and loathed, attitudes were still sufficiently permissive that the controlled distribution of synthetic opiates such as methadone to confirmed addicts became acceptable.
Head shops, purveying intriguing and attractive paraphernalia for the storage, preparation and ingestion of drugs, emerged as symbols of the apparent acceptance of drug use. Therein lies the danger.
Thus, the paraphernalia industry is a merchandising outgrowth of the phenomena of the expansion of so-called recreational drug use in the United States and Canada over the last 25 years. The industry's history really begins in the counter culture movement of the United States during the mid 1960's, which most Members will recall. Its development parallels the emergence of "alternative lifestyles" which were reflected in the credo developed by the "guru" of the sixties, Dr. Timothy Leary who encouraged the youth of North America to "tune in, turn on and drop out". 1 wonder how many lives were destroyed with that simple misguided philosophy.
Much of this counter-prevailing attitude was fostered by a substantial degree of disfavour with the involvement of the United States in the Vietnam conflict. Anyone old enough will remember the spill-over effect of this conflict into Canada. Clearly 1 recall it because much of the spill-over effect was felt in Kootenay West. The occupation and destruction of equipment at the computer centre of Sir George Williams University in Montreal in 1969 is a classic example which comes to mind. It was a time of considerable malaise in North America. It was a time of social confusion and absence of direction.
Extensive use of marijuana, cocaine and other drugs has created enormous social, health and legal problems. There are factions that proclaim the dangerous consequences of all nonmedical drug use as well as those that advocate the legalization and availability of all substances. I would certainly oppose the use of these dangerous drugs.
Other lobby groups for the reform of marijuana laws have been active. In certain American states, civil fines have been substituted for criminal penalties resulting from possession of small amounts of marijuana. There are persuasive studies to show that the use of marijuana may be more harmful than thought 10 or 20 years ago. Yet it continues to be a cash crop in my riding, referred to as "Kootenay Green".
January 28, 1988

One of the more visible repercussions of the drug revolution has been the multimillion dollar industry that has developed to supply the equipment used to grow, process, store, conceal and use illicit drugs and to profit from the demands of their customers. The manufacturers, most of whom are in the United States, and retailers of these implements associated with so-called recreational drug use are new entrepreneurs who acknowledge, thankfully, the precarious nature of their prosperity and unfortunately capitalize on their connection with illegal activities of the illicit drug industry.
"Paraphernalia" is not a precise term. Even when limited to drugs, paraphernalia can refer to equipment for legal or illegal administration of legal or illegal substances. For example, hypodermic needles can be used to inject medically approved drugs as well as illicit substances such as heroin. Alligator clips that have a legitimate use in the electronic and hobby industry are also perfectly suited as a "roach clip" in the smoking of marijuana cigarettes. A kitchen spoon becomes drug paraphernalia when used to snort cocaine and cook heroin. There is a great deal of difficulty, therefore, in defining exactly what is drug paraphernalia.
The industry that manufactures, distributes and sells the drug paraphernalia has limited itself to the creation of an enormous and varied number of products primarily related to the two most frequently used drugs, marijuana and cocaine. A minor interest has been shown in equipment to grow psychedelic mushrooms and to cultivate opium and various herbs, spices and teas. Generally, the paraphernalia industry does not involve itself in the selling, displaying, advertising or in any way glamorizing implements for making, storing, or administering so-called hard drugs. This includes syringes, "cookers", needles, gear for making veins more prominent and thus more easily injectable, powder-like substances for diluting narcotics, purifying equipment, and the like. However, there are complaints of products such as free-base kits for use in cocaine consumption that demonstrate a willingness on the part of these enterprises to enter the hard-drug field.
In any event, we must consider what to do in relation to any use of paraphernalia associated with all illicit drugs. What has not been mentioned so far in this debate is that the use of these syringes and needles for the injection of drugs often means, in the drug addict community, a sharing of the needle or syringe. It is in that fashion that the deadly virus, commonly referred to as AIDS, is transmitted. So, apart from the application of some of this paraphernalia for the sole purpose of taking drugs, there is, as a consequence, in some parts of our society, a very terrible risk of the continued escalation of the virus AIDS.
The Drug Paraphernalia Model Act which was developed by the American Department of Justice, which was expected to deal with the broad problem of drug paraphernalia, has been subjected to a considerable number of court challenges. The rationale behind these court challenges is really quite simple. The description or definition of "paraphernalia" is excessively
Illicit Drugs Promotion
vague and imprecise, thus, the model Act runs afoul of the U.S. Constitution's Fourteenth Amendment's guarantee of due process. The problem is clearly stated in the judgment of the United States Court of Appeal, Seventh Circuit, in 1982: He reads:
The difficulty that has plagued draftsmen of drug paraphernalia ordinances is how to control traffic in drug-related equipment without also proscribing wholly innocent conduct. Mirrors, spoons, pipes and cigarette papers are all multiple-purpose items. A statute that has no ambiguities will reach only the most obvious items of drug paraphernalia, while a statute that casts a broader net may be too vague.
While the United States Supreme Court upheld the constitutionality of a similar definition of paraphernalia in a regulatory scheme requiring the registration of paraphernalia sales, the court has not ruled on the model Act's attempt to prohibit and criminalize the paraphernalia trade. The national drug strategy announced by this Government in May of last year, 1 hope will resolve the problem. It is a multi-faceted attack on the drug problem in Canada. The development and funding of innovative approaches to the demanding side of the problem by means of education programs, including media communication, are now operating for all to see. In addition, I am hopeful that the specific use of drug paraphernalia which is now being addressed by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Hnaty-shyn) will add further enlightenment to the process.
Drug paraphernalia availability is a matter that concerns all the citizens of Canada. It concerns this Government, and this Government, in my view, will act upon it in a responsible way to the satisfaction of responsible Canadian citizens.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-BILLS   CRIMINAL CODE MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first, I would like to praise the concern expressed in this Bill by its proponent. I think it can be said that most Canadians share his concern about the issue of drug abuse in Canada.
I would just like to say that it is important to recognize that quite recently a report of the Standing Committee on National Health and Welfare entitled Booze, Pills and Dope was released, which dealt with the issue before us today. Given what has been said in reference to this Bill, 1 think it is important to refer to the report because a good deal of what is said reflects a stereotyping of drug abuse. In oral testimony and in briefs presented to the standing committee, witnesses expressed special concern about the extent and severity of the abuse of alcohol which, it became clear from those representations, is the most widely abused drug in Canada, to the extent of around 95 per cent. Perhaps there is an error in focus here. In fact, we seem inclined to ignore the real problems, and those problems, in addition to alcohol, would include the over-the-counter sale of legal drugs that are abused far more than marijuana or cocaine.
I would like to point out that a great many recommendations were made in our report which, by the way, had the unanimous agreement of representatives from all Parties with no one dissenting. 1 would just like to say that there are a number of recommendations one might have hoped would have

January 28, 1988
Illicit Drugs Promotion
become the subject of a Private Member's Bill. If we are to refer to the issue of drug paraphernalia, I think we should take note of the recommendation and commentary which was made with respect to drug paraphernalia in this report. The development of legislation aimed at banning drug paraphernalia is a difficult task as in most cases items of drug paraphernalia also have legitimate and non-drug applications. It was therefore recommended that instead of attempting to outlaw the ordinary items used in connection with drug use, some legislative attempt be made at dealing with the issue of head shops.
The standing committee recommended that the Minister of Justice, in co-operative efforts with his provincial counterparts, develop legislation to close head shops, commercial enterprises whose principal business is the sale of drug paraphernalia and items which describe their use and which advocate the use of illicit drugs. With respect to Bill C-264, I have to say that its drafting is almost bizarre. It is so poorly drafted that if it were to pass, I would have to suggest it would call Parliament into disrepute. It would outlaw as an instrument for illicit drug use:
-anything designed primarily or intended under the circumstances for
consuming or to facilitate the consumption of an illicit drug;
Literature for illicit drug use would also be outlawed. That means any printed matter describing or depicting and designed primarily or intended under the circumstances to promote or glamorize the production, preparation or consumption of illicit drugs. According to this suggested legislation the following items would perforce be outlawed; cigarette papers, razor blades, pipes, water pipes or otherwise, syringes, hypodermics, electrical clips, bobby pins, cigarette holders, glass tubing, rubber tubing, cigarette machines, mortars and pestles, and I am told by some, even twenty dollar bills, brand new, of course.
Let us also consider the history of literature with respect to drug use. Under some circumstances as described in this Bill, we would outlaw the following literature; A Rebours by Joris-Karl Huysman, Kubla Khan, A Vision in a Dream by Samuel Taylor Coleridge, Ulalume by Edgar Allen Poe, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes by Sir Arthur Conan Doyle, Alice in Wonderland, by Louis Carroll, Tropic of Capricorn by Henry Miller, Naked Lunch by William S. Burroughs, On the Road by Jack Kerouac, Howl and Other Poems by Allen Ginsberg, Beneath the Underdog by Charles Mingus and The Collected Works of Billy the Kid by Michael Ondaatje, winner of the Governor General's Award for Poetry in 1971.
This legislation is a sloppy bit of draftsmanship. It should not be accepted as such. However, that does not mean that we reject the notion that an effort should be made to ban head shops. There is a possibility that that approach would have some merit. But, of course, it is outside the jurisdiction of the federal Government. It resides at the provincial level and at the municipal level.
I would commend to the Minister of Justice that, in lieu of this Bill being enacted, means be explored, with the other levels of Government, to bring about a practical attack on the matter of drug paraphernalia as it can only be done through legislation aimed at head shops.
I would like to make one more plea. If we are going to deal with the issue of drug abuse, then let us be conscious of the fact that, although it conjures up all kinds of fears and visions of kids smoking dope on the street, the real issue in Canada is not the abuse of marijuana or of cocaine, however dangerous it may be, but the abuse of alcohol by all too many without full cognizance of the dangers involved in its use and the tragedy that has been costing so many lives. If we want to do some good, then we should read the report entitled, Booze, Pills and Dope. Let us act on that. If we follow the recommendations in this report which reflect the knowledge of those who have been involved in the issue of drug abuse then we might indeed make some material progress.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-BILLS   CRIMINAL CODE MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am glad to be able to participate in this debate. I want to begin by saying that I agree with my colleague, the Hon. Member for Windsor-Walkerville (Mr. McCurdy), that there is a lot wrong with this Bill. That is to say that it could be extended to a degree which, as we have seen from American experience with similar Bills, would make it totally unworkable. Such items as hairpins, safety pins, books and ashtrays, as well as many other products which are innocently used in one character can be not so innocent when used in another. There will always be a problem to ensure that the subject matter is covered precisely in a Bill so that our criminal law is as clear as possible.
While it is possible to draft the Bill in a better fashion I think there is a good idea contained in it. It would be constructive to see this Bill move forward, perhaps with similar Bills which are on the Order Paper. In this way a committee could look at the issue to see whether it is possible to define with some precision a class of products whose identification with drug use is so close that it would be fair to criminalize their sale.
I would like to achieve that result because I believe that a very peculiar signal is being given by the existence and character of head shops to people across the country. We were told by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) about one year ago that there was a drug epidemic in Canada. Perhaps that was an exaggeration. Perhaps it was a bit of grandstanding by the Prime Minister. However, when we look at it we ought to be prepared as a society to do what we can to deter drug use.
Head shops are hard to explain to young people when trying to tell them that the use of hard and soft drugs is undesirable and that they ought to try to avoid their use. I want to use the criminal law not only to deter harmful conduct but to a certain extent send a signal about our views as a community on drug use.
January 28, 1988

At the present time we are looking at Bill C-51 which deals with the smoking of tobacco which is also a harmful drug. It is not a mood-altering or mind-bending type of drug but it is harmful and a killer. While considering this Bill we are also entitled to look at the use of drugs, hard and soft, and the type of paraphernalia that is associated with their use. I am not sure whether such a goal is attainable. The burden is on the mover of the Bill, on those who favour it and witnesses who come forward to convince us that we would not be launching a witch- hunt and criminalizing the use of innocent products. If a means could be found, I think it would be desirable to stop sending such a signal out and to take steps to see that we stop tolerating the use of hard and soft drugs by permitting easy access to products uniquely associated with their consumption in one form or another.
I would like to remind the House, and perhaps it has already been done, that a parliamentary committee looked at drug abuse. It made a unanimous report. That report included support for legislation of this type. It was a very general recommendation and I do not like general amendments to the Criminal Code. I want specific amendments to the Criminal Code. However, I have in mind as a goal the improvement of the signal that we are sending to young people about drug use.
I would like to conclude by saying that if one wanted to challenge me I know that making these products illegal will not stop drug use and perhaps not even reduce the access to drugs or to associated products by those who are looking for them. One cannot reduce the amount of smoking that goes on in society just by banning ashtrays or matches. That is something which no sensible person would suggest. But in this case I think there is a signal being sent out at a time when young people make their minds up about whether they want to try these products before they are addicted to them. Before they become the socially in-thing for them and their set to do I would like them to get a proper signal from the community that we oppose them.
This is a Private Member's Bill. I am only speaking for myself. However, I know that a great many of my colleagues in the Liberal Party share these concerns. We would welcome further study of the Bill in an attempt to try to find a proper descriptive formula for classifying products which could be banned, something which we are trying to do in the area of tobacco smoking.
May I call it six o'clock, Mr. Speaker?

subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-ARCTIC CO-OPERATION-PROPOSALS MADE BY SOVIET UNION LEADER
EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-ARCTIC CO-OPERATION-PROPOSALS MADE BY SOVIET UNION LEADER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it was on October 1 of last year that Mikhail Gorbachev, the leader of the Soviet Union, made a very major speech in Murmansk in the far northwest of the Soviet Union on the Kola Peninsula, a town which is familiar to certain Canadians. It is evident that a great deal of thought and preparation went into that presentation. There were a number of new policy initiatives contained therein.
What Mr. Gorbachev was trying to do on that occasion was to take a polar view of the world rather than the view which is more familiar. He was trying to look down on the world from the polar region so to speak. He made six major points in his presentation.
The first two dealt with defence issues and contained a lot of the normal rhetoric which one expects. It is quite clear that the people in the Soviet bloc do not trust us in the western bloc any more than we really trust them. We would both like to work toward disarmament and a lessening of tensions, but at the same time we both want to keep our defences up. He made reference to a northern nuclear free zone at some point in time. He realized that it could not happen overnight, and he suggested methods by which this might be achieved over a number of years, or how we might start discussions toward that end. It is somewhat ironic that this proposal came from the Kola Peninsula, one of the most heavily armed parts of the world, which is literally bristling with arms. His ideas might carry a little more weight were the Soviet Union to cease and desist from sending their Bear H. bombers over to my riding.
Also he proposed in the defence field possible restrictions on naval activity in certain northern waters, or at least mechanisms leading toward that end, such as agreements on notification of naval manoeuvres and the possibility of having observers when those manoeuvres take place.
What I really want to talk about is the other four proposals in the non-military field. There was a proposal concerning cooperation in developing the natural resources of the North- oil, gas, and minerals in particular. There were offers made of possible joint business projects which might take place in the northern part of the Soviet Union. There was a proposal for a

January 28, 1988
Adjournment Debate
joint Arctic Scientific Council. The Soviet Union, Canada, the United States, Finland, Sweden, and Norway would be the logical participants, together with Greenland and Denmark, of course.
There was a suggestion that social sciences might be discussed as well as the physical sciences. Usually scientific cooperation with the Soviet Union has dealt with the physical sciences and engineering. They have been extremely reluctant to discuss the social sciences, history, ethnology, or that type of thing because they have their Own views on those particular subjects. It does not seem that they want those views contaminated by some of the views which we have in the West. It is a new initiative to talk about co-operation, especially in the field of the social sciences.
Another point was co-operation on environmental protection, which is important in the North-both water or marine protection and the necessity for having clean air in the North. A lot of contaminants seem to gravitate toward northern areas.
He proposed an extension of the system which is in place in the Baltic Sea where I understand there is a commission comprised of the seven states that border the Baltic Sea and where they co-operate to reduce environmental pollution in that particular body of water.
He suggested the possible opening up of northern sea routes with lots of ice-breaker protection, et cetera. He suggested the possible opening up of the Northeast Passage along the northern coast of the Soviet Union, which would go hand in hand with what we have in mind with the opening up of the Northwest Passage at some point in time. On January 11 we concluded an agreement with the United States of America toward that end, co-operation on navigation in arctic waters. These were important proposals that were made in Murmansk.
1 know, because I was in the Soviet Union with the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) some years ago, that there are existing agreements dealing with scientific and cultural exchanges. These are good and are working reasonably well. There is no reason that we cannot improve upon them, extend and invite more countries to get involved, the other northern countries, Scandinavia, the United States, et cetera.
[DOT] <1805)
There has been a fair amount of diplomatic follow-up on this speech by Soviet diplomatic staff here in Ottawa. Shortly after the speech had been made, I had the pleasure of meeting with the Minister Counsellor from the U.S.S.R., Mr. Alexei Makarov. He impressed upon me the importance of this speech. I think that a formal response should be forthcoming from the Government of Canada to address some of these points that have been raised. I hope that can take place in the not-too-distant future.

speakeroldname: Mr. Jean-Guy Hudon (Parliamentary Secretary to Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-ARCTIC CO-OPERATION-PROPOSALS MADE BY SOVIET UNION LEADER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the proposals
contained in the speech made on October 1, 1987, in Murmansk by Secretary General Gorbachev were recently developed further in a speech given by Soviet Premier Ryzhkov in Oslo on January 14. However, in our opinion, the Soviet Premier added but a few new elements to the speech of Mr. Gorbachev.
As indicated by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) in his speech of December 9 at the Norway-Canada Conference on Circumpolar Issues, we wish for the development of a pacific cooperation between the countries of the Arctic Basin, and we are therefore heartened by the statement made by Secretary General Gorbachev in Murmansk on October 1. We have especially noted his suggestion of co-operation in the areas of energy, science and environment."
We are pleased to learn that the Soviet Union is interested in the establishment of an Arctic Scientific Council, a project in which Canada, Norway and other countries are involved.
He also added this: We have especially noted his interest in the development of cultural ties among Northern people. We hope that the Soviet Union will accept for the first time to participate in the Inuit Circumpolar Conference in 1989, as well as the Inuit Youth Camp in 1988, which will be hosted by Canada.
However, we have asked for more detailed information about what the Soviet's interest means for all practical purposes. Moreover, we shall continue to pursue our own objectives and defend our interest in the Arctic.
Our military capabilities in the North are all defensive and will remain so. The nuclear submarines which we are buying will help identify and oppose all ennemy naval activities in the Arctic, especially under the ice cap. However, the comments made by Mr. Gorbatchev and Mr. Ryzhkov do not reflect the actions of their Government. Contrary to Canada and other Northern countries, the Soviet Union has an enormous concentration of military power and weapons in the Arctic. Especially in the Kola Peninsula region where is stationned a large part of its fleet of submarines equiped with strategic missiles. The denuclearized northern zone proposed by the Soviets would not effect these forces. We believe that negotiations first and foremost offer the best hopes of a reduction, to an acceptable level, of nuclear arms and a better balance of conventional forces.

Mr. Speaker, I rise with regard to a question I asked on December 9, 1987 about the Government's mismanagement, incompetence and possible corruption relating to the disposition of lands in the Mirabel Airport area. This is in connection with resales of land to former farmers, former tenants, the farmers being the original
January 28, 1988

owners and to land speculators, many of whom as events have unfolded are Tory Party organizers or Tory Party supporters.
1 asked a tough question not only because of the allegations which have come out, some of which are already the subject of lawsuits relating to the company, but because the Mirabel Land Corporation had failed to file its financial statements. According to the Auditor General, it was the only Crown corporation which had failed to file its corporate statements during the time and on time as provided.
The Canadian people have seen a lot of scandals associated with this Government. Some of them are before the criminal courts, some of them have been dealt with by special inquiries. This one is in part already before the courts in a civil suit.
1 would like to remind the House what this civil suit is about. A farmer whose land was expropriated claims that he was offered his land back provided he would flip it to a Tory organizer who operated a quarry. When he agreed to flip the land at a small mark-up which was settled in an agreement he was asked to keep secret, he consulted his Member of Parliament, and the media tell us that his Member of Parliament told him to keep his mouth shut and not complain or he would not get the land. When the land was transferred, not only did he get the 80 hectares of which he had originally been expropriated but he got 320 hectares, I believe, and so it went throughout the entire scandalous disposition of this land.
I want to give the Government more opportunity than the ordinary Question Period provides to explain itself. 1 do not think the explanations that government Members have been giving so far are washing. The explanations they are giving involve alleged improper sales or improper conduct on the part of the Liberal Government, the preceding Government, in the way this project was put together. One can see that that is not a logical defence.
There is no reason for what was done before this Government took office in connection with land deals to excuse the type of conduct and behaviour we are criticizing in the House of Commons. However, government Members have not even gone so far as to explain why they consider the conduct of the former Government scandalous.
When we were the Government, one thing we did have was a pretty vigilant operation. The people who are now in Government were the Opposition. In that entire period, I cannot recall, with all the efforts they made to damage the Government of the day, to find scandals and to force Ministers to resign, anything arising from this that at the time was used to successfully or otherwise damage us.
I suggest that the kinds of defences and explanations government Members have been using-

Member will have a chance to answer, and I am looking forward to hearing the kind of answer that will condone or excuse the type of behaviour that we on this side of the House have been criticizing. Mrs. Shirley Martin (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister
of Public Works): Mr. Speaker, the question the Hon. Member for York Centre (Mr. Kaplan) asked in the House on December 9, 1987 contained two items: one, the filing of the annual report, and two, the so-called dismissal of the board at that time. The Hon. Member stated that the Canada Lands Company had broken the law by failing to file its Annual Financial Return statement by last June. The Minister explained previously that discussions with the Auditor General were being concluded and that he would have the information tabled at the first opportunity. The Minister tabled the Financial statements on December 14, immediately following his receipt of the required Auditor General's accompanying letter. The entire annual report of the corporation was then tabled on January 18, 1988, when the House reconvened.
It is obvious that you cannot close a corporation's books for the year while the auditors are there and you cannot have the financial statements finalized until the auditor's report is complete. So to say that the company broke the law is rather misleading. Perhaps the timing requirements of the Financial Administration Act in this regard are a bit too rigid and should be looked at. The point is that the Minister provided the House with all information and fulfilled all of his statutory obligations in this regard at the earliest possible opportunity. That is fact.
The Member might want to note that under the previous Liberal Government, which he said administered the country so well, the financial statements for the years ending 1982 and 1983 were not tabled until mid-1984, unbelievably late by today's standards. They were not considered late by the Liberals then because they had not bothered to have any such legal requirements. It is clear that the Opposition's record on these matters is poor.
What is of more importance is that the board of directors was not "fired by the Government" and replaced last summer, as alleged by the Hon. Member for York Centre. It has been well established over past weeks that the Minister made several improvements over the past months in certain administrative practices of the corporation. Various audits and reviews did identify minor deficiencies, but basically the corporation's record is a very good one. The corporation has done extremely

One of the actions the Minister took was to make three new board appointments in July, 1987. This was in response to the observation of the Auditor General that all the members of the board consisted of officers of the corporation. The new appointments were made to broaden the board's representation to include the federal Public Service and the private sector. The appointments were not made in criticism of the then board members, but to eliminate any possible perception of a conflict of interest.
The direction of the company was not changed in August, 1987, as the Hon. Member suggested. SHIPBUILDING-INQUIRY WHEN SIX FRIGATES WILL BE BUILT/REQUEST THAT MINISTER OF FINANCE MEET REPRESENTATIVES OF SHIPBUILDING INDUSTRY

subtopic: CANADA LANDS COMPANY-ALLEGED FAILURE TO FILE ANNUAL FINANCIAL RETURN-REQUEST THAT ANNUAl REPORT BE PRESENTED BY NEXT MONDAY AT LATEST
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on November 4 I asked questions in the House relating to the Canadian shipbuilding industry. I asked about the awarding of a second contract for the construction of six patrol frigates for the Canadian Navy. I also pursued removal of the exemption from duty of large fishing boats, a policy of the previous Liberal Government which has been continued by the present Government. The answers were quite unsatisfactory and reflected the failure of the Conservative Government to develop policy for the shipbuilding industry. In my few minutes this evening I want to address the importance of proper and open planning to the shipbuilding industry in Canada, a need which the Government has failed so lamentably to recognize, it seems.
The plight of the industry of course needs little elaboration. There is very little commercial work to be done other than repair of vessels. There is a great deal of unemployment in every community where a shipyard or a related facility has long been in existence. The only possibility that exists under the present Government's inactive policy is that government work may, as was true in the last days of the Trudeau Government, provide some opportunity for employment in a variety of shipyards. The question is: How many yards will be able to use government contracts in order to keep men at work and keep those companies in operation?
In this context, I want to express my astonishment at the Government's decision just days before Christmas past to award the second half dozen patrol frigates entirely to the Saint John shipyard. That was truly an incredible decision which went against all the expectations aroused in Quebec and which betrayed, I assert, the assurances given to the people of Quebec. It created an enormous amount of ill feeling up and
down the St. Lawrence Valley against the present Conservative Government. In response to the Member for Montreal- Sainte-Marie (Mr. Malepart) on November 4, 1987, in specific relation to the matter of the frigate contracts, the Minister of Supply and Services (Mr. Cote) said:
We will continue to defend the interests not only of Quebecers but of all
Canadians as well.
That is one of those famous statements which deserves to be carved in stone up and down the St. Lawrence Valley with regard to that particular contract.
It is particularly repugnant to Quebecers to see one particular enterprise, the Irving interests in Saint John, receiving this very large contract to the detriment of the provincially owned Marine Industries Limited with yards up and down the St. Lawrence.
The other point that I was determined to make had to do with the refusal of the Government to consider a removal of the exemption of large fishing boats from the payment of duty. That exemption is now justified to be removed. The fishing industry is in good shape and there is a possibility that construction of large vessels for the fishery could be carried on in Canada in Atlantic yards for which the Government seems to have such tender feelings.
The refusal of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) even to meet with Marine Industries early in 1987, when planning was going forward on the Budget that he brought forward last February, is simply incredible. It indicates the blindness of the Government in one particular area where commercial work might be developed for Canadian yards. In the Minister's absence again, unfortunately, I want to make the point again that that is one of the items which the Government should be looking at as it considers the Budget for 1988.
In this context, although undeclared, we have seen a policy of rationalization which means closure of yards. It has been most obvious in Ontario where the Admirable Yard, a century old in Collingwood, had to be closed. As a result, ship building and ship repair operations in the Province of Ontario are now entirely controlled by one company. I note again that when the Minister was responding to my question, he spoke of the need to provide healthy competition in order to encourage regional development. There is no healthy competition left in the Province of Ontario.
Rationalization along the St. Lawrence became obvious to us first in the spring of 1986 when a letter came to the attention of the public which made it clear that there was to be a rationalization which is now being carried through under the compulsion which the Government, by its lack of policy, has imposed on the industry. As a result of that, building will be carried on only at Lauzon. Sorel may be involved in the construction of modules for vessels. Vickers is completely out of the maritime industry under this policy. That is the
January 28, 1988

consequence of the lack of policy which the Government has had.
The possibility that there will be naval work of sorts is still an entirely open question. The Government's determination to build a certain number of nuclear submarines will soak up incredible amounts of public funds. Will we see the patrol vessels and minesweepers built which could provide work in other yards? Surely it would be far better to have conventional submarines at less cost and other vessels including perhaps another half dozen patrol frigates.
In conclusion, we need a process of open dealings with the industry and consultation with the public, workers, and management in order to establish the policies which could put shipbuilding on a sound basis and continue it with prosperity into the 1990s.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to respond to the concerns raised by my colleague from Thunder Bay-Nipigon (Mr. Epp). The Government's strategy regarding shipbuilding and repair is clear and precise. We have two primary objectives which guide our policy, the rationalization of our shipbuilding industry and regional development. The awarding of the frigate contract to Saint John Shipbuilding proves the Government's commitment to these objectives.
We are all aware of the considerations that led to the announcement that took place in late December. In reaching this decision, our Government took into account that in 1983, Saint John Shipbuilding Limited had obtained the prime contract through the competitive bidding process. Thus the Government did not have to draw up a new contract, it simply added a modification to the old one.
Over the course of the past four years a great deal of time, energy and money has been invested in order to develop installations and expertise and to improve the over-all administrative structures necessary to execute the work. During a period of fiscal constraint, we have endeavoured to avoid repeating unnecessary expenditures and to take advantage of
Adjournment Debate
what we already possess. It is evident that these reasons of economy, efficiency and expertise helped determine the Government's decision.
Similarly, the design, construction and integration of the weapons-control systems-work amounting to approximately $800 million-will be carried out, as in the case of the first six frigates, by Paramax Electronics of Montreal.
The award of the frigate contract again demonstrates the Government's firm commitment to making procurement work for the economic development of Canada as a whole. For example, the sub contracts that will go to other companies will bring industrial benefits to many regions of Canada. Part of that contract will be handled by a firm in Hamilton adjacent to my riding in Ontario. It is estimated that in the second phase of this project 50 per cent of the benefits will go to Atlantic Canada; 24 per cent to Quebec; and 26 per cent to Ontario and western Canada.
Calculated over the entire life of the 12-ship project, the breakdown is slightly different: 37 per cent to Atlantic Canada; 33 per cent to Quebec; and 30 per cent to Ontario and western Canada. Over the course of the next nine years, the construction of the six patrol frigates will represent the equivalent of 14,000 person-years of employment, with more than half of the jobs going to workers in the Atlantic region alone where employment opportunities are most welcome.
Our Government is pleased that the Atlantic region will benefit so much. At the same time, we are pleased with the benefits in which all Canadians will share.
In closing, the announcement of the patrol frigate contract to Saint John Shipbuilding confirms their status as a centre of excellence for Canadian shipbuilding.
